kbs.etymology: KBS is an initialism of Korean Broadcasting System, the broadcaster in this scene. Its official institutional history distinguishes the beginning of radio broadcasting in 1927 from its establishment as a public broadcaster in 1973.
kbs.notes: The Korean letter-name reading is 케이비에스. This is an institutional name history, not a claimed Korean lexical root.

sources.title: KBS — official English institutional introduction

신입사원.etymology: A Sino-Korean expression built from 신입 (新入, newly entering) and 사원 (社員, company staff member). The Basic Dictionary records the phrase as 신입 사원 with the characters 新入社員; the source dialogue writes it as one unit.
신입사원.notes: This documents the compound structure, not a first-attestation date. In 신입사원이시죠, the noun is followed by a respectful confirmation: the speaker checks the listener’s identity.

아.etymology: An independent Korean reaction interjection. The Basic Dictionary distinguishes this spoken reaction word from the identically written name of the vowel letter; its uses include recognition, surprise and opening a remark.
아.notes: Here it is a brief reaction before an explanation. The cited dictionary establishes its word class and present uses, not a remote historical derivation; no Chinese-character ancestry or ancient date is asserted.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — Korean Basic Dictionary: 아 — interjection

네.etymology: The polite answer 네 has documented older spelling variants, but its derivation is unresolved. NIKL’s historical-dictionary response records 녜 in a 1940 dictionary as equivalent to 네, and in the 1947–1957 Big Dictionary as equivalent to 예. NIKL explicitly reports finding no etymological explanation.
네.notes: These are recorded variant/equivalence statements, not proof that 네 developed from 예. The source uses the respectful yes, not the same-spelled pronoun or numeral.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — Korean Basic Dictionary: 네 — affirmative interjection

왜.etymology: The reason-question adverb 왜 is the word meaning why in this exchange. The Basic Dictionary separates it from a confirmation interjection, a vowel-letter name and a Chinese-character homograph.
왜.notes: The documented lexical distinction matters here: 왜 asks for the reason for running. The cited entry does not establish a deeper historical root, so an origin from the unrelated character 倭 is not claimed.

sources.title: National Institute of Korean Language — Korean Basic Dictionary: 왜 — reason adverb

뛰다.etymology: The running verb 뛰다 has its own Basic Dictionary entry, distinct from the separately listed jumping verb with the same spelling. Here its stem 뛰- takes the respectful ending -세요 in a question about the visible running.
뛰다.notes: This is a present-day word-family and inflection explanation. The two dictionary entries do not by themselves prove a historical derivation of running from jumping; no such chronology is asserted.

morphemes.meaning: respectful question here; other contexts can give a request

저.etymology: 저 is the humble first-person pronoun, distinct from the demonstrative meaning that. Its subject form is 제가 and its possessive is 제; these belong to the pronoun’s established present-day paradigm.
저.notes: The cited dictionary supports the pronoun family, not an explanation of its earliest creation. This entry does not invent a Chinese-character origin or derive it from the demonstrative homograph.

입사식.etymology: A transparent Sino-Korean compound: 입사 (入社, joining a company) plus -식 (式, a ceremony). The Basic Dictionary documents 入社 in 입사하다 and lists a ceremony-forming sense of the suffix -식, distinct from its method/style sense.
입사식.notes: The formation identifies a new-employee induction ceremony. It does not mean Seung-chan is the person organizing it, and these component entries do not supply a first-attestation date for the complete compound.

하다.etymology: The basic Korean action verb 하다 supplies the do/perform part of many event expressions. Its stem 하- appears in 하는데요, with a background-setting ending and polite listener marking: the event explains the speaker’s hurry.
하다.notes: The cited dictionary distinguishes the main verb from auxiliary uses. This note explains the current formation rather than claiming a documented ancient source for the stem.

늦다.etymology: The dictionary distinguishes verbal 늦다, arriving or acting later than a set time, from descriptive 늦다, a time or season being late. This scene concerns the scheduled induction. In 늦은 거, the stem 늦- has a modifier ending before the bound noun.
늦다.notes: This is the documented modern lexical distinction and source formation. No date or unattested remote etymology is inferred from the two present-day entries.

것.etymology: The bound noun 것 can package a thing, fact or situation. NIKL explicitly identifies 거 as its spoken form. The same explanation records 게 when this spoken form combines with the subject particle, and 거다 with the copula.
것.notes: The source keeps the actual colloquial 거 in 늦은 거 같아가지고. It need not have its own separate English translation. The documented spoken/written relationship is not a claim about the earliest origin of 것.

같다.etymology: 같다 has documented comparison and sameness uses and also occurs in an impression pattern with a preceding clause and 것. The source uses colloquial 거 followed by 같아가지고 to give an impression as the reason for running.
같다.notes: These are coexisting dictionary senses, not a dated claim that one historically developed from another. The spoken ending in this scene is preserved instead of being silently replaced with a more formal connective.
